knowledge_point.title: Determining the Units of a Derivative

question.:question/problem: Mary bakes $c$ cupcakes using $f(c)$ grams of flour. What are the units of $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}c}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have that the amount of flour $f(c)$ is measured in grams and the number of cupcakes is measured in cupcakes. 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(c): & \text{grams} \\ c: & \text{cupcakes}\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}c}$ measures a change in $f(c)$ over a change in $c.$ So, it represents a ratio of the units:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}c}: & \frac{\text{grams}}{\text{cupcake}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}c}$ is measured in "grams per cupcake".

question.:question/problem: A dairy farm sells milk on a particular day for $p(v)$ dollars, where $v$ is the number of liters of milk in the dairy farm at the start of the day. What are the units of $\frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}v}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have that the price $p(v)$ is measured in dollars and the volume of milk is measured in liters. 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(v): & \text{dollars} \\ v: & \text{liters}\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative $\frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}v}$ measures a change in $p(v)$ over a change in $v.$ So, it represents a ratio of the units:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}v}: & \frac{\text{dollars}}{\text{liters}}\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, $\frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}v}$ is measured in "dollars per liter".

question.:question/problem: A farmer estimates that she can sell $w(p)$ metric kilograms of crops at a price of $p$ dollars per kilogram. What are the units of $\frac{dw}{dp}$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have that $w(p)$ is measured in kilograms and $p$ is measured in dollars per kilogram. 

$$
\begin{aligned}w(p): & \text{kilograms} \\ p: & \text{dollars per kilogram}\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative $\frac{\text{d}w}{\text{d}p}$ measures a change in $w(p)$ over a change in $p.$ So, it represents a ratio of the units:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}w}{\text{d}p}: & \frac{\text{kilograms}}{\text{dollars per kilogram}}=\frac{\text{squared kilograms}}{\text{dollars}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\frac{\text{d}w}{\text{d}p}$ is measured in "squared kilograms per dollar".
